overview:
A string of harbour towns on the eastern Mediterranean coast — roughly modern Lebanon, with edges in coastal Syria and northern Israel — grew rich on the narrow shelf between the Lebanon mountains and the sea. Byblos was trading cedar to Egypt in the third millennium BCE, and Tyre, Sidon and Arwad joined it as centres of a Canaanite coastal world long before Greeks gave the region the name that stuck. "Phoenicia" is a Greek coinage, probably from phoinix, the purple-red of the dye extracted from crushed murex shells that became the coast's most famous export. The people it describes did not use it of themselves. They called themselves Canaanites, identified first by city and family, and left no evidence of a shared national identity or of a state that united them. Most scholars therefore treat "Phoenician" as a convenience for the period after about 1200 BCE, when the collapse of the Bronze Age empires left these cities free to expand into the trading vacuum.

What followed was less an empire than a commercial network. Phoenician shipwrights and navigators worked the whole Mediterranean, carrying timber, glass, dyed cloth, worked ivory and metals, and acting as intermediaries between Egypt, Mesopotamia, the Aegean and the far west. From perhaps the ninth or eighth century BCE — the chronology is genuinely disputed, since early trading posts leave little in the ground — permanent settlements appeared on Cyprus, Sardinia, Sicily, Malta, the North African coast and southern Iberia. Carthage, traditionally founded from Tyre around 814 BCE, eventually eclipsed its mother city and built an empire of its own. Meanwhile the homeland cities spent centuries as tributaries: to Assyria from the campaigns of Shalmaneser III in the ninth century, to Babylon, whose siege of Tyre dragged on from roughly 585 to 573 BCE, and then to Persia after 539 BCE, where they supplied the fleets that fought Greece while keeping considerable local autonomy. Alexander broke Tyre after a seven-month siege in 332 BCE with famous brutality, and the coast passed through Hellenistic hands before Rome absorbed it in the 60s BCE, when Pompey reorganised Syria.

The most consequential thing these cities exported was not a commodity. Their consonantal alphabet, compact enough to be learned by merchants rather than a scribal class, was adapted by the Greeks — who added vowels — and through them became the ancestor of Latin, Cyrillic, and by other routes Aramaic, Syriac, Hebrew and Arabic scripts. It travelled the same routes as the cargo.
significance: Almost every alphabet in use today descends from the script these traders carried; the writing you are reading is a distant Phoenician descendant. Beyond that, the Phoenician cities pioneered a model of power that was commercial rather than territorial — a web of harbours, agreements and diasporic communities rather than a conquered interior — and in doing so knitted the Mediterranean into a single economic space for the first time. Their western settlements seeded Carthage, Cádiz and Palermo, and the Punic world that grew from them became Rome's most dangerous rival, so that the shape of the Roman Mediterranean was partly determined by where Tyrian merchants had chosen to anchor centuries earlier.
coverage: This dataset holds no events at all for Phoenicia, so the overview is written entirely from reference works rather than from anything the map can display; readers should treat the chronology here as summary, not as sourced points. The deeper problem is the record itself: the Phoenicians wrote on papyrus, and almost none of it survives, so the civilization is known largely through Egyptian, Assyrian, Hebrew, Greek and Roman writers who were variously trading partners, overlords or enemies, plus archaeology. Dates for the earliest colonies, the founding of Carthage, and the span's own 2499 BCE opening are all inferred or traditional rather than firmly attested.
